So why not renting? It’s still a chore to get utilities set up, buy renters insurance, get air filters changed, handle pest control, and more.

That’s why we’ve built the world’s first Resident Experience Platform that makes resident onboarding, resident services, and ancillary revenue effortless for property managers.

We’re passionate about turning friction into triple win experiences for residents, property managers, and investors. That way renting can be easy and rewarding for everyone.

And now you can join us. Apply today to join 300+ passionate, creative people who strive to make a difference each day so residents, property managers, and investors all win – creating the ultimate Triple Win.

Role Snapshot

Second Nature is seeking a senior product executive to lead Product Management as a portfolio of businesses. This is the most senior product management role at the company, reporting to the Chief Product & Technology Officer with regular, direct exposure to the CEO/Founder and executive team given the strategic weight of the portfolio.

This role leads a team of Group Product Managers, each accountable for a product line as a business. Working with that group as general managers of their product lines to drive business outcomes is central to the job.

Why This Role Exists

Benefits

Second Nature is converting strong bookings growth into long-term enterprise value by expanding the Resident Benefits Package category. This leader owns whether expansion happens, through a Product Management organization accountable for unit economics, revenue, and retention. The scoreboard:

Attach rates across the core portfolio, with the mechanisms understood well enough to repeat as product lines expand
The share of new revenue carried by newer product lines, broadening the portfolio beyond its current base
Retention and new logo acquisition, with clear attribution to the work that drove them
Unit economics across the portfolio, improved without trading away growth
A roadmap that is a rationalized allocation of investment against business outcomes, resourced to execute and delivered against

This is a business leadership role first, expressed through outstanding product management. The right person is as fluent discussing customer lifetime value, unit economics, and market opportunity as they are discussing a roadmap or a discovery plan.

They read a business review the way an operator does - what is working, what is not, and what needs to change - and translate that read into clear direction for the leaders and teams who report to them. This leader treats product excellence as something measured by customer experience as well as business outcomes and holds the same standard across the portfolio.

Discovery is funded as protected capacity, and prioritization is running on demand-side customer data
Investment is focused on what customer evidence supports, and the organization understands the reasoning

Commercial Curiosity: Asks what moves revenue and what customers will pay for before asking what to build

Talent Multiplier: Raises the bar on product talent and develops product managers into general managers of their lines
Bias to Action Under Ambiguity: Moves decisions forward with imperfect information, and is energized rather than destabilized by speed and ambiguity
Evidence Over Conviction: Changes direction when customer evidence contradicts the plan, including when the plan was theirs
Cross-Functional Authority: Aligns GTM, Finance, Operations, and Engineering behind portfolio priorities using business logic those functions recognize, and carries Product Management's point of view on company-level questions that extend beyond its control
Extreme Ownership: Owns the outcome, not the handoff - stays accountable when the result depends on work outside their control

Cross-Functional Partnerships

This role's success depends on four partnerships, each with a clear division of ownership:

Engineering: Peer partnership on capacity, feasibility, and delivery. Product sets business outcomes and priorities; Engineering owns technical execution
Finance and RevOps: Unit economics, line-level attribution, pricing, and portfolio margin
Go-To-Market: Positioning, distribution strategy, new logo acquisition, and attach-rate mechanisms

jobs.title: Principal Product Manager — Ecosystem
jobs.description:
About Us

Fanatics is building a leading global digital sports platform. We ignite the passions of global sports fans and maximize the presence and reach for our hundreds of sports partners globally by offering products and services across Fanatics Commerce, Fanatics Collectibles, and Fanatics Betting & Gaming, allowing sports fans to Buy, Collect, and Bet. Through the Fanatics platform, sports fans can buy licensed fan gear, jerseys, lifestyle and streetwear products, headwear, and hardgoods; collect physical and digital trading cards, sports memorabilia, and other digital assets; and bet as the company builds its Sportsbook and iGaming platform. Fanatics has an established database of over 100 million global sports fans; a global partner network with approximately 900 sports properties, including major national and international professional sports leagues, players associations, teams, colleges, college conferences and retail partners, 2,500 athletes and celebrities, and 200 exclusive athletes; and over 2,000 retail locations, including its Lids retail stores. Our more than 22,000 employees are committed to relentlessly enhancing the fan experience and delighting sports fans globally.

The Role

Fanatics operates as a set of separate companies — Betting & Gaming, Commerce, Collectibles, Live, Retail — that happen to share the same fans. Our team's job is to make those companies feel like one thing to a fan: one identity, one loyalty currency, one set of habits, and a platform underneath that means we build an experience once and deploy it everywhere.

This is the widest product seat we have. It runs from the surfaces a fan actually touches — the Fanatics app, scores, free-to-play, the places loyalty shows up — down to the infrastructure that makes any of it work across five businesses. You'll own both ends, and the connection between them is where most of the value is.

It is also the role we point at the hardest open problem in the ecosystem. When something matters and nobody owns it, or someone owns it and it's stuck, you go in, get deep enough to actually solve it, and then either keep it or hand it off cleanly and move to the next one.

If you want one product area and a settled roadmap, this is the wrong job. If the best work you've done was the work nobody had scoped yet, keep reading.

What You'll Own

The Fanatics app and the daily habit

The app is the front door to the ecosystem for millions of fans, and scores are why a lot of them open it. A scores product on its own is a utility. The opportunity is a daily habit that earns the right to be the first app someone checks, and then carries them into everything else we do. You'll own the questions that decide whether that happens: what a fan sees first, what brings them back tomorrow, and how following a game turns into a bet, a card, a ticket or a conversation with their friends without feeling like a funnel.

How We Get Fans In

Registration, onboarding and the first session. Cross-sell that works because it's relevant rather than because someone bought a merchandising slot. Referral and invite mechanics. A single login across every product — which is a growth number for us, not a hygiene metric, because every extra front door a fan has to sign up at costs us a share of them.

How We Keep Them

Habit loops, and being honest about which of ours actually loop. What gives a fan a reason to open something on a Tuesday in February. Notifications that earn their place rather than spend down our credibility. Cohort retention by product and by entry point, and the work of finding where we lose people and fixing it rather than reporting it.

Free-to-play

Free-to-play is the workhorse of this ecosystem. It's the top of the funnel for regulated products, the thing that still works in states where we can't take a bet, the mechanic that keeps a fan engaged between wagers, and the lowest-risk way for someone to learn how our products work. You'll own where it goes next: game design, cadence, prizing, how it ladders into the paid products, and what it's genuinely worth as an acquisition and retention channel rather than what we assume it's worth.

How Loyalty Shows Up

FanCash is the currency that connects the ecosystem, and most of its value is in how it surfaces in-product. There is a large gap between a loyalty programme that exists and one a fan can feel. You'll own the earn and burn moments inside the apps, how the bonus engine shows up on each surface, and whether a fan actually understands what they've got and what it's for. This is where loyalty either compounds or stays a line item in a settings menu.

Scaling the infrastructure — build once, deploy everywhere

Identity, the shared SDK and our common components exist so that five businesses stop building the same thing five times. You'll own pieces of that platform and, harder, its adoption: persuading op-co teams to take a shared component instead of writing their own, and making it good enough that taking it is the obvious choice. You'll also be in the room on scale — what breaks at ten times the traffic, where the service boundaries should sit, and what we need to build now so that 2027 isn't a rewrite.

The biggest problems in the ecosystem

The rest of the role is the swing mandate. The ecosystem generates more high-value, unscoped problems than we have people to point at them. You'll take the ones that matter most, go deep enough to solve them rather than triage them, and then either keep the area or hand it over

Challenges We're Not Going To Hide From You

Fanatics really does operate as separate companies, with their own P&Ls, roadmaps and priorities. You'll have significant influence and almost no authority. If that sounds like an excuse for things not moving, this will be frustrating. If it sounds like the interesting part, you'll do well here.
Breadth is the risk as well as the appeal. Spread across everything and you add nothing. A real part of this job is refusing work and being able to defend the refusal to people who outrank you.
FanCash and free-to-play straddle betting/gaming and commerce, which means legal and compliance constraints that vary by state, by product and sometimes by partner. Some of your best ideas will die on regulatory grounds. You'll need to find the next-best version quickly and without sulking about it.
Inbound demand far exceeds capacity. Deciding what we won't do is most of the prioritisation work.
Data and analytics maturity in this area is a known gap. We'd like the person in this seat to help close it rather than wait for someone else to.

How We Measure Success

Fanatics ONE account growth
Retention and repeat-visit rates in the app
Free-to-play participation, and its measured contribution to acquisition and retention of the paid products
FanCash earned and burned, the number of op-cos where FanCash is usable, and whether fans understand what they've earned
Shared component adoption, measured in duplicate builds avoided
Rate at which fans move from a first product into a second and third
Decision quality in the areas you own

What You Bring

The combination we're after is rare, and it's the whole point of the role: someone who has built consumer products that fans love and
platform products that other teams depend on.

Eight or more years in product, with genuine consumer product ownership and genuine platform or infrastructure ownership. Both — not one with exposure to the other
Range, evidenced. You've owned meaningfully different problems, and you get useful in an unfamiliar domain in weeks rather than quarters
You've carried acquisition or retention numbers and can defend what actually moved them
Technical depth to be a real partner to platform engineering: APIs, SDKs, authentication and identity flows, data models, service boundaries, and what breaks under load. You don't need to have written the code. You do need to hold your own in a design review and know when an estimate sounds wrong
Data fluency you can demonstrate. You write your own queries, you design experiments that answer the question you actually have, and you know the difference between a metric moving and a metric mattering

jobs.description:
About Us

Fanatics is building a leading global digital sports platform. We ignite the passions of global sports fans and maximize the presence and reach for our hundreds of sports partners globally by offering products and services across Fanatics Commerce, Fanatics Collectibles, and Fanatics Betting & Gaming, allowing sports fans to Buy, Collect, and Bet. Through the Fanatics platform, sports fans can buy licensed fan gear, jerseys, lifestyle and streetwear products, headwear, and hardgoods; collect physical and digital trading cards, sports memorabilia, and other digital assets; and bet as the company builds its Sportsbook and iGaming platform. Fanatics has an established database of over 100 million global sports fans; a global partner network with approximately 900 sports properties, including major national and international professional sports leagues, players associations, teams, colleges, college conferences and retail partners, 2,500 athletes and celebrities, and 200 exclusive athletes; and over 2,000 retail locations, including its Lids retail stores. Our more than 22,000 employees are committed to relentlessly enhancing the fan experience and delighting sports fans globally.

The Role

Fanatics is building a connected ecosystem where fans can move across Betting & Gaming, Collectibles, Live, FanApp and more, powered by a single identity, a shared loyalty system, and common product experiences.

We are looking for a senior product leader to build the social and community layer of that ecosystem. This is a growth job. One fan meets us across our products and is alone in all of them. We pay to acquire them four times and we work to keep them four times. The room to grow inside what we already own is bigger than anything more media spend or an additional vertical would get us.

Social is how we connect it. Fandom is a group activity and our products treat it as a solo one. Profiles, friends, groups, sharing, competition and status are the mechanics that bring acquisition cost down, carry a fan from one product into the next, and give people a reason to come back that isn't another push notification.

The other half of it is knowing who the fan is. We know who someone roots for, what they collect, what they've sat through as a fan. That turns a cross-sell into recognition, and it lets us answer a moment in one product with something real from another. It's a network of fans who are known and connected to each other organically.

You will own social end to end: the thesis, the roadmap, the mechanics, the growth numbers and the gamification layer that sits on top.

Why This Role Matters

Today our products are social in name only. Fans arrive alone, play alone, and leave without having met anyone. Every vertical acquires and retains its own users, discovery runs on merchandising slots rather than on what a fan's friends are doing, and identity mostly resets at every front door a user enters here. The result is separate funnels where there should be one network.

As the product leader for Growth, Social & Community, you will:

Define where ecosystem growth comes from and which social mechanics unlock it
Build identity and public profile as a real product
Create acquisition loops that come out of the product itself
Turn shared experience into a retention mechanic the whole ecosystem benefits from
Make the value of a social lever measurable enough to fund

Your work will directly affect blended acquisition cost, cross-product penetration and retention, Fanatics ONE membership and engagement, and the rate at which fans move from their first product into their second and third.

What You'll Do

Own the growth thesis and the roadmap

Write the point of view: where the growth comes from, which social mechanics get us there, what each one is worth, and the order to build them in.
Keep a live read on where consumer social is going and what it means for us.

Build acquisition that doesn't come out of the media budget

Invite, referral and friend discovery built into the product rather than sitting next to it.
Sharing that fans actually want to do, which means moments worth sending rather than a share button bolted on
Social surfaces that put Fanatics in front of people who aren't customers yet

Connect the ecosystem through identity and the social graph

Identity and a public social profile built as a real product: who someone is across verticals, who they root for, what they collect, what they're good at, carried with them instead of reset at every front door.
Reputation and a record worth showing off to all fans
One social graph that every vertical uses instead of each building its own.
Discovery driven by what a fan's friends are doing
A privacy model where being public is a choice and a safe one.

Design for moments rather than campaigns

Fandom runs on highs and lows, and the ecosystem gives us both the signal to see them and the means to respond.
Work from context and not just behavior, understand what happened to a fan and how the fan feels about it.
Bring generosity, perfect timing, and a bias toward being on the fan's side

Build community that keeps people around

Shared experience, including the plain fact of knowing that thousands of other fans are sitting in the same moment you are, sweating it together.

Own the gamification layer

Progression that means something
Group and squad competition, what makes a fan recruit their friends.
A clear position on where rewards genuinely change behavior and how to introduce

Prove it with data

Define what a social lever is worth
Density against retention, invite and share loops against acquisition cost, cross-product LTV, and what a second and third product per fan is actually worth.

The Bar

We are not trying to catch up. We intend to be where this happens for sports fans, and we have the fan base and the ecosystem to make that the clear outcome. You are expected to know what is shipping in that space before it ships, and to tell us what it means for us.

You will be working with a small, strong, AI-forward team that moves quickly. Keeping pace with them is part of the job. In practice that means you prototype, you get something in front of fans this week, and you don't wait on a sprint cycle to think and make decisions.

How We Measure Success

Reduction in blended acquisition cost attributable to in-product social loops
Share of fans connected to at least one other fan, and density on the surfaces that matter
Rate at which fans move from a first product into a second and third
Retention and engagement lift among connected fans versus unconnected ones
Fanatics ONE membership growth and login adoption across products
Adoption of shared social and identity components by partner teams

What You Bring

Eight or more years in product, with real time on growth and real time on social, community or network products at consumer scale
Social products rather than social features. Things where the value came from other users, and you know how graphs get built
You've carried a growth number and can defend a roadmap to it
Both ends of the funnel. Acquisition and retention
The ability to write the narrative that gets a company aligned, and to sit with two engineers and a designer and get something in front of users this week
You build fast. Prototypes over specs, days over quarters, and you cut things quickly when they don't work
You use consumer social products and have opinions about them. You also understand how fans behave, the loyalty and the superstition and the heartbreak
You decide at 80%, write down why, and change your mind when the data says to
You can write the query, design the test, debate incrementality with a data scientist, and tell a real lift from a seasonal one
You've dealt with the ugly side of user-generated content before - moderation, abuse, bad actors

Things That Make Us Lean Forward

A social product you shipped that outlived the team that built it
A graph you grew from nothing, and a clear story about how you solved cold start
Users you moved between products or business units at scale
Something you built that made people feel recognized
Something you killed because the data said to
Three social products you admire, why each loop works, and where each one breaks
Work across P&Ls where you owned the outcome but not the roadmap
Something public. A product, a repo, writing, a community you started and grew
Experience shipping social or UGC inside a regulated or high-scrutiny environment

Why You'll Love This Role

You'll build the social layer for one of the largest fan bases in sports
The vision is yours to write, and it comes with real investment behind it
Your work shows up across every Fanatics product rather than inside one of them
You'll work with strong partners across Product, Design, Engineering and Data
There is a shipping v1 to learn from and an open 2027 to define

No resume. No cover letter. Run the entire process in Claude Code. The session pulls in how you operate. You add your background, and it generates your submission. Clone the repo at https://github.com/centrfit/centr-growth-product then run /apply in Claude Code.

Welcome to Centr - The Home of Strength

Centr is a performance fitness platform founded by Chris Hemsworth. We sell connected fitness equipment, digital training subscriptions, and bundles that combine both. We're the official equipment provider for HYROX.

Our subscription business is the engine, and the funnel doesn't yet deliver. Mobile converts respectably; web converts far below it. Paid acquisition costs more than a product this good should have to spend. And the biggest opportunity is hiding in plain sight: equipment buyers, customers who already paid us hundreds or thousands of dollars and unlocked a free trial as part of their purchase, convert at a fraction of other channels. The people who signaled the highest intent are opportunities we're losing. We're not asking you to optimize a mature funnel. We're asking you to build one.

About the role

You own the subscription funnel from the moment a user encounters Centr through their first 30 days of paid usage. Web pages between ad click and trial start, in-app onboarding through first workout, offer architecture at trial end, cancellation, and the in-app surfaces that drive equipment upsell once they're a subscriber. You'll work next to the Sr. Ecom Manager (storefront, CRM, bundle), our growth agency (paid acquisition), and the Core UX product team (long-term in-app experience).

A dedicated full-stack web engineer is paired to you, and the two of you ship the web funnel autonomously. Paywalls and pricing iterate via RevenueCat config without dev tickets. Native mobile work routes through Core UX engineering, so part of your job is making the case for prioritization rather than assuming the capacity.

We move these numbers by building experiences worth converting on. Our read is that the funnel underperforms because the experience does, not because we haven't pushed hard enough. We'd rather earn a subscription than trap someone into one. Get the experience right and the numbers follow.

What you'll own

Web subscription onboarding. Signup, assessment, paywall, offer, trial activation. Closing the conversion gap between web and mobile is a first-90-days priority.
QR-to-app landing. The post-scan experience for retail equipment buyers (Costco, Academy) and bundle buyers.
In-app activation. Install through day 7. Onboarding flow, day-0/1/3 nudges, push, in-app engagement during trial.
Trial-to-paid conversion. Offer architecture at trial end, in-app re-engagement, cancellation on web and in-app, win-back surfaces inside the product.
Pricing and packaging. Plan architecture across iOS, Android, and web. Differentiated offers for new vs. returning vs. lapsed users.
In-app equipment upsell. The shopping feature, placement, and surfacing logic that turns subscribers into bundle and equipment buyers.

What success looks like

Web trial conversion closes a meaningful share of the gap to mobile
iOS install → paid conversion improves materially against today's baseline
A QR-to-app flow we're excited to point Costco and Academy traffic at
An in-app equipment upsell surface producing measurable attach from existing subscribers
A cancellation flow that recovers a respectable share of would-be churners
CAC payback shortened enough that paid spend can scale with confidence

You should apply if

You've owned a subscription funnel end-to-end and moved trial-to-paid at consumer scale
You've shipped against both mobile (iOS/Android) and web subscription flows and understand why they behave differently
You know where the landmines are in RevenueCat, App Store / Play Store, Stripe, and Recharge
You believe the best growth work is indistinguishable from the best product work. You move trial-to-paid by making the trial deliver value, not by hiding the cancel button
You're effective at influencing roadmaps you don't own (a meaningful chunk of your highest-leverage work lives inside the Core UX roadmap)
You spend more time in Claude Code than anyone you know

This might not be the right fit if

Your experience is all with mature, well-instrumented funnels. Building one from zero is a different muscle, and this role is mostly the zero-to-one kind
You love CRO and landing-page work but don't want to own pricing, paywalls, and trial design alongside it
You'd rather hit targets with pressure tactics than earn them through the experience
You want to own strategy and hand off execution. Here you'd do both
You want a proven playbook to run. We're still writing ours, and that's the fun of it

Why this role

Centr's subscription business has the brand, the content, the equipment, and the HYROX tailwind. What it's missing is someone to own the funnel that ties them together. If building that sounds like the best problem you could be working on, we'd like to meet you.

new_jobs.description:
About Us

Fanatics is building a leading global digital sports platform. We ignite the passions of global sports fans and maximize the presence and reach for our hundreds of sports partners globally by offering products and services across Fanatics Commerce, Fanatics Collectibles, and Fanatics Betting & Gaming, allowing sports fans to Buy, Collect, and Bet. Through the Fanatics platform, sports fans can buy licensed fan gear, jerseys, lifestyle and streetwear products, headwear, and hardgoods; collect physical and digital trading cards, sports memorabilia, and other digital assets; and bet as the company builds its Sportsbook and iGaming platform. Fanatics has an established database of over 100 million global sports fans; a global partner network with approximately 900 sports properties, including major national and international professional sports leagues, players associations, teams, colleges, college conferences and retail partners, 2,500 athletes and celebrities, and 200 exclusive athletes; and over 2,000 retail locations, including its Lids retail stores. Our more than 22,000 employees are committed to relentlessly enhancing the fan experience and delighting sports fans globally.

The Role

Fanatics operates as a set of separate companies — Betting & Gaming, Commerce, Collectibles, Live, Retail — that happen to share the same fans. Our team's job is to make those companies feel like one thing to a fan: one identity, one loyalty currency, one set of habits, and a platform underneath that means we build an experience once and deploy it everywhere.

This is the widest product seat we have. It runs from the surfaces a fan actually touches — the Fanatics app, scores, free-to-play, the places loyalty shows up — down to the infrastructure that makes any of it work across five businesses. You'll own both ends, and the connection between them is where most of the value is.

It is also the role we point at the hardest open problem in the ecosystem. When something matters and nobody owns it, or someone owns it and it's stuck, you go in, get deep enough to actually solve it, and then either keep it or hand it off cleanly and move to the next one.

If you want one product area and a settled roadmap, this is the wrong job. If the best work you've done was the work nobody had scoped yet, keep reading.

What You'll Own

The Fanatics app and the daily habit

The app is the front door to the ecosystem for millions of fans, and scores are why a lot of them open it. A scores product on its own is a utility. The opportunity is a daily habit that earns the right to be the first app someone checks, and then carries them into everything else we do. You'll own the questions that decide whether that happens: what a fan sees first, what brings them back tomorrow, and how following a game turns into a bet, a card, a ticket or a conversation with their friends without feeling like a funnel.

How We Get Fans In

Registration, onboarding and the first session. Cross-sell that works because it's relevant rather than because someone bought a merchandising slot. Referral and invite mechanics. A single login across every product — which is a growth number for us, not a hygiene metric, because every extra front door a fan has to sign up at costs us a share of them.

How We Keep Them

Habit loops, and being honest about which of ours actually loop. What gives a fan a reason to open something on a Tuesday in February. Notifications that earn their place rather than spend down our credibility. Cohort retention by product and by entry point, and the work of finding where we lose people and fixing it rather than reporting it.

Free-to-play

Free-to-play is the workhorse of this ecosystem. It's the top of the funnel for regulated products, the thing that still works in states where we can't take a bet, the mechanic that keeps a fan engaged between wagers, and the lowest-risk way for someone to learn how our products work. You'll own where it goes next: game design, cadence, prizing, how it ladders into the paid products, and what it's genuinely worth as an acquisition and retention channel rather than what we assume it's worth.

How Loyalty Shows Up

FanCash is the currency that connects the ecosystem, and most of its value is in how it surfaces in-product. There is a large gap between a loyalty programme that exists and one a fan can feel. You'll own the earn and burn moments inside the apps, how the bonus engine shows up on each surface, and whether a fan actually understands what they've got and what it's for. This is where loyalty either compounds or stays a line item in a settings menu.

Scaling the infrastructure — build once, deploy everywhere

Identity, the shared SDK and our common components exist so that five businesses stop building the same thing five times. You'll own pieces of that platform and, harder, its adoption: persuading op-co teams to take a shared component instead of writing their own, and making it good enough that taking it is the obvious choice. You'll also be in the room on scale — what breaks at ten times the traffic, where the service boundaries should sit, and what we need to build now so that 2027 isn't a rewrite.

The biggest problems in the ecosystem

The rest of the role is the swing mandate. The ecosystem generates more high-value, unscoped problems than we have people to point at them. You'll take the ones that matter most, go deep enough to solve them rather than triage them, and then either keep the area or hand it over

Challenges We're Not Going To Hide From You

Fanatics really does operate as separate companies, with their own P&Ls, roadmaps and priorities. You'll have significant influence and almost no authority. If that sounds like an excuse for things not moving, this will be frustrating. If it sounds like the interesting part, you'll do well here.
Breadth is the risk as well as the appeal. Spread across everything and you add nothing. A real part of this job is refusing work and being able to defend the refusal to people who outrank you.
FanCash and free-to-play straddle betting/gaming and commerce, which means legal and compliance constraints that vary by state, by product and sometimes by partner. Some of your best ideas will die on regulatory grounds. You'll need to find the next-best version quickly and without sulking about it.
Inbound demand far exceeds capacity. Deciding what we won't do is most of the prioritisation work.
Data and analytics maturity in this area is a known gap. We'd like the person in this seat to help close it rather than wait for someone else to.

How We Measure Success

Fanatics ONE account growth
Retention and repeat-visit rates in the app
Free-to-play participation, and its measured contribution to acquisition and retention of the paid products
FanCash earned and burned, the number of op-cos where FanCash is usable, and whether fans understand what they've earned
Shared component adoption, measured in duplicate builds avoided
Rate at which fans move from a first product into a second and third
Decision quality in the areas you own

What You Bring

The combination we're after is rare, and it's the whole point of the role: someone who has built consumer products that fans love and
platform products that other teams depend on.

Eight or more years in product, with genuine consumer product ownership and genuine platform or infrastructure ownership. Both — not one with exposure to the other
Range, evidenced. You've owned meaningfully different problems, and you get useful in an unfamiliar domain in weeks rather than quarters
You've carried acquisition or retention numbers and can defend what actually moved them
Technical depth to be a real partner to platform engineering: APIs, SDKs, authentication and identity flows, data models, service boundaries, and what breaks under load. You don't need to have written the code. You do need to hold your own in a design review and know when an estimate sounds wrong
Data fluency you can demonstrate. You write your own queries, you design experiments that answer the question you actually have, and you know the difference between a metric moving and a metric mattering
Cross-organisational influence where you owned the outcome but not the roadmap. Multi-brand, multi-P&L, holding-company, super-app or marketplace environments are directly relevant
Comfort in a regulated environment. You've shipped inside legal and compliance constraints and treated compliance partners as collaborators rather than obstacles
Writing strong enough to carry a decision without you in the room. This matters more here than in most PM jobs
Low ego and a bias to action. You pick things up, you close them out, and you don't need credit assigned before you'll start
The judgment to go deep on the right thing — and, harder, to stop working on the wrong one

Things That Make Us Lean Forward

A consumer app where you owned a daily-habit or retention metric and moved it, with the curve to show it
Free-to-play, fantasy, predictions or games-of-skill experience, especially where it fed a paid product
Loyalty, rewards or membership experience across multiple brands, including the economics: liability, breakage, margin, and what a point is actually worth
You've built or scaled an identity, auth or accounts platform used by several products
You've driven internal adoption of a shared platform against teams who'd rather build their own — and can describe exactly how you won
You've been handed the ambiguous, politically complicated problem more than once, on purpose
You've killed something you built
You've worked somewhere the ecosystem was the product: a super-app, a multi-vertical marketplace, a multi-brand membership programme
A document you wrote that changed what a company decided to do

This Role Is Probably Not For You If

You want a single product area and a settled roadmap
You need authority to be effective
You're a consumer PM who thinks platform work is a step down, or a platform PM who'd rather not talk to fans
You read "wide" as permission not to go deep. This role needs both, and the depth is the harder half
You're uncomfortable working on someone else's priority when it's clearly the right thing for the ecosystem
You'd rather own a roadmap than solve a problem

Why You'll Love This Role

The widest view of the Fanatics ecosystem of any product seat we have, and the shortest path to seeing your work in front of millions of fans
You'll own consumer surfaces and the platform underneath them, which very few product jobs let you do
Real scope now, and a clear path to owning a charter of your own
You'll work directly with the person running the area, with their air cover
Identity, loyalty and the app are the things every op-co needs, which means your work compounds instead of shipping once and going quiet
One of the largest fan bases in sports, and a genuine chance to make five companies feel like one

Through the Fanatics platform, sports fans can buy licensed fan gear, jerseys, lifestyle and streetwear products, headwear, and hardgoods; collect physical and digital trading cards, sports memorabilia, and other digital assets; and bet as the company builds its Sportsbook and iGaming platform. Fanatics has an established database of over 100 million global sports fans; a global partner network with approximately 900 sports properties, including major national and international professional sports leagues, players associations, teams, colleges, college conferences and retail partners, 2,500 athletes and celebrities, and 200 exclusive athletes; and over 2,000 retail locations, including its Lids retail stores. Our more than 22,000 employees are committed to relentlessly enhancing the fan experience and delighting sports fans globally.

The Role

Fanatics is building a connected ecosystem where fans can move across Betting & Gaming, Collectibles, Live, FanApp and more, powered by a single identity, a shared loyalty system, and common product experiences.

We are looking for a senior product leader to build the social and community layer of that ecosystem. This is a growth job. One fan meets us across our products and is alone in all of them. We pay to acquire them four times and we work to keep them four times. The room to grow inside what we already own is bigger than anything more media spend or an additional vertical would get us.

Social is how we connect it. Fandom is a group activity and our products treat it as a solo one. Profiles, friends, groups, sharing, competition and status are the mechanics that bring acquisition cost down, carry a fan from one product into the next, and give people a reason to come back that isn't another push notification.

The other half of it is knowing who the fan is. We know who someone roots for, what they collect, what they've sat through as a fan. That turns a cross-sell into recognition, and it lets us answer a moment in one product with something real from another. It's a network of fans who are known and connected to each other organically.

You will own social end to end: the thesis, the roadmap, the mechanics, the growth numbers and the gamification layer that sits on top.

Why This Role Matters

Today our products are social in name only. Fans arrive alone, play alone, and leave without having met anyone. Every vertical acquires and retains its own users, discovery runs on merchandising slots rather than on what a fan's friends are doing, and identity mostly resets at every front door a user enters here. The result is separate funnels where there should be one network.

As the product leader for Growth, Social & Community, you will:

Define where ecosystem growth comes from and which social mechanics unlock it
Build identity and public profile as a real product
Create acquisition loops that come out of the product itself
Turn shared experience into a retention mechanic the whole ecosystem benefits from
Make the value of a social lever measurable enough to fund

Your work will directly affect blended acquisition cost, cross-product penetration and retention, Fanatics ONE membership and engagement, and the rate at which fans move from their first product into their second and third.

What You'll Do

Own the growth thesis and the roadmap

Write the point of view: where the growth comes from, which social mechanics get us there, what each one is worth, and the order to build them in.
Keep a live read on where consumer social is going and what it means for us.

Build acquisition that doesn't come out of the media budget

Invite, referral and friend discovery built into the product rather than sitting next to it.
Sharing that fans actually want to do, which means moments worth sending rather than a share button bolted on
Social surfaces that put Fanatics in front of people who aren't customers yet

Connect the ecosystem through identity and the social graph

Identity and a public social profile built as a real product: who someone is across verticals, who they root for, what they collect, what they're good at, carried with them instead of reset at every front door.
Reputation and a record worth showing off to all fans
One social graph that every vertical uses instead of each building its own.
Discovery driven by what a fan's friends are doing
A privacy model where being public is a choice and a safe one.

Design for moments rather than campaigns

Fandom runs on highs and lows, and the ecosystem gives us both the signal to see them and the means to respond.
Work from context and not just behavior, understand what happened to a fan and how the fan feels about it.
Bring generosity, perfect timing, and a bias toward being on the fan's side

Build community that keeps people around

Shared experience, including the plain fact of knowing that thousands of other fans are sitting in the same moment you are, sweating it together.

Own the gamification layer

Progression that means something
Group and squad competition, what makes a fan recruit their friends.
A clear position on where rewards genuinely change behavior and how to introduce

Prove it with data

Define what a social lever is worth
Density against retention, invite and share loops against acquisition cost, cross-product LTV, and what a second and third product per fan is actually worth.

The Bar

We are not trying to catch up. We intend to be where this happens for sports fans, and we have the fan base and the ecosystem to make that the clear outcome. You are expected to know what is shipping in that space before it ships, and to tell us what it means for us.

You will be working with a small, strong, AI-forward team that moves quickly. Keeping pace with them is part of the job. In practice that means you prototype, you get something in front of fans this week, and you don't wait on a sprint cycle to think and make decisions.

How We Measure Success

Reduction in blended acquisition cost attributable to in-product social loops
Share of fans connected to at least one other fan, and density on the surfaces that matter
Rate at which fans move from a first product into a second and third
Retention and engagement lift among connected fans versus unconnected ones
Fanatics ONE membership growth and login adoption across products
Adoption of shared social and identity components by partner teams

What You Bring

Eight or more years in product, with real time on growth and real time on social, community or network products at consumer scale
Social products rather than social features. Things where the value came from other users, and you know how graphs get built
You've carried a growth number and can defend a roadmap to it
Both ends of the funnel. Acquisition and retention

You build fast. Prototypes over specs, days over quarters, and you cut things quickly when they don't work

You can write the query, design the test, debate incrementality with a data scientist, and tell a real lift from a seasonal one
You've dealt with the ugly side of user-generated content before - moderation, abuse, bad actors

Things That Make Us Lean Forward

A social product you shipped that outlived the team that built it
A graph you grew from nothing, and a clear story about how you solved cold start
Users you moved between products or business units at scale
Something you built that made people feel recognized

Three social products you admire, why each loop works, and where each one breaks
Work across P&Ls where you owned the outcome but not the roadmap

Experience shipping social or UGC inside a regulated or high-scrutiny environment

The vision is yours to write, and it comes with real investment behind it
Your work shows up across every Fanatics product rather than inside one of them

Job Description:

YOUR MINDSET

You have spent your career becoming fluent in disciplines most people keep separate. You don't see creative strategy and media strategy as different languages. You see them as different expressions of the same strategic thinking. That mastery is what qualifies you for this role.

You believe that the best ideas scale, that coherence matters more than novelty, and that the team creating the strategy is as important as the strategy itself. You lead with conviction and curiosity. You build a culture where people think bigger about their work because they get excited about it.

Role Overview

You will develop and execute a range of integrated strategy projects for a specific brand or strategic focus area within a multi-brand consumer healthcare enterprise, translating strategic direction into inspirational insights and briefs that enable great creative and media execution come together.

This role demands fluency in two disciplines that most separate: Brand Strategy and Connected Strategy. You work from both perspectives simultaneously. You don't just translate between them, you hold them together with clear strategic thinking that helps them operate as one. You understand how strategy needs to live across earned, owned, and paid channels—including social and influencer partnerships.

You turn strategic direction into clear big ideas and briefs grounded in audience insight and media possibility. You work with creative and media teams to help them understand how their work fits together into a coherent whole and inspire both to think bigger and think together. You are the bold strategic voice in the room who helps teams see how their work connects and why that connection matters.

Core Responsibilities

Strategic Boldness: Ideas & Brief

Shape and create the Catalyzing Idea(s) that will help orchestrate across three distinct business units with sophistication and specificity
A builder of brand worlds that dimensionalize ideas- articulating character, conviction, and edges with rigor and specificity that drives great creative work
Develop the strategic narratives that help enterprise leadership understand not just what you're doing, but why it matters and how it moves their business
Bring the same strategic depth to idea development as to system deployment. The ideas are the work. They are not secondary to execution, and brave ideas matter.

System Orchestration : The Deployment

Architect an Intelligent Story System: defining WHERE ideas reach the right audiences across all three business units and orchestrating HOW they show up in context
Identify audience signals that inform where and when each idea becomes urgent and inevitable
Ensure that as the system expands across channels, moments, and audiences, coherence never breaks. Every execution- whether retail media, pharmacy communications, or insurance education- radiates from the same idea
Lead creative, media, product, and retail teams to rally around the idea itself, not fracture into tactics. Help them understand they're part of something bigger than their discipline, and why their piece matters to the whole.

Cross-Brand Enterprise Leadership

Hold the enterprise perspective. You are the leader who sees where all three brands can move together and where they must move independently
Identify strategic opportunities where one idea scales across all three business units (creating compounding effect) and where each business unit needs its own force (creating specificity)
Create conditions where the three brands strengthen each other, not cannibalize each other

Media + Creative Integration at Strategic Foundation

Think in both languages simultaneously, from idea through deployment. You are fluent in creative strategy AND media strategy- not choosing between them, but weaving them together around an idea
You understand how media strategy informs which ideas can scale, which audiences you can reach, where cultural moments live. You understand how creative strategy demands certain media contexts to land. You hold both truths at once
Brief media and creative leaders not as separate functions receiving strategy, but as strategic partners who help shape how ideas move in the world

Relationship Growth

Build and steward a mission-critical relationship by delivering integrated work that creates visible business impact for enterprise leadership
Position yourself as the strategic authority the enterprise turns to when the question is "how do our brands behave?" or "what's the opportunity we're missing?"
Create the conditions where integrated strategy becomes not a nice-to-have, but fundamental to how their enterprise operates

Team Building & Leadership Development

Help assemble and lead a world-class team that embodies integrated thinking at every level
Recruit for depth, not just breadth. You want strategists who are genuinely fluent in both creative and media thinking, not people who dabble in both
Develop the next generation of strategists who understand systems thinking, not just tactical execution
Create psychological safety where team members are empowered to challenge siloed thinking and contribute strategic ideas, not just execute briefs
A servant leader. Your actions help create our culture

Measurement, Learning & System Optimization

Help monitor how strategy translates in market and gather feedback for refinement
Support measurement that tracks whether the system is working, using data as feedback not just reporting
Contribute insights on how ideas are propagating and whether signals are clustering as predicted

What Success Looks Like

Your ideas are clear enough that a junior strategist can explain them. They're sophisticated enough that a CEO pauses and says "yes, that's what we're trying to do."
Creative and media strategies are inseparable. You cannot explain one without the other. The team describes them as one thing
All three business units operate from shared ethos while maintaining distinct expressions where it makes sense. The coherence is visible; the differentiation is clear
Your team thinks in systems. They understand signal stacking. They see how their work feeds the whole. New team members are onboarded into a way of thinking, not just a project
You have recruited and developed strategists who will lead integrated thinking across the agency- your legacy is multiplication
Measurement shows that ideas are proliferating, signals are clustering as predicted, and the system is compounding over time
The relationship grows because integrated strategy has become indispensable to how they operate. They ask for more

Proven ability to develop and communicate breakthrough strategic thinking, not just execute briefs
Track record working on consumer or B2C brands in complex strategic environments
Experience working across creative and media functions
Comfort engaging with senior stakeholders in strategic conversations
Experience with social media platforms and/or influencer partnerships a plus

Understanding of how systems work- not just campaigns, but interconnected strategic systems
Comfort holding complexity: three brands, multiple audiences, multiple signals, one coherent force

Evidence that you think about how ideas propagate and compound, not just how they perform in a single moment

Note special application requirements:
No resume. No cover letter. Run the entire process in Claude Code. The session pulls in how you operate. You add your background, and it generates your submission. Clone the repo at https://github.com/centrfit/centr-growth-product then run /apply in Claude Code.

Welcome to Centr - The Home of Strength

Centr is a performance fitness platform founded by Chris Hemsworth. We sell connected fitness equipment, digital training subscriptions, and bundles that combine both. We're the official equipment provider for HYROX.

Our subscription business is the engine, and the funnel doesn't yet deliver. Mobile converts respectably; web converts far below it. Paid acquisition costs more than a product this good should have to spend. And the biggest opportunity is hiding in plain sight: equipment buyers, customers who already paid us hundreds or thousands of dollars and unlocked a free trial as part of their purchase, convert at a fraction of other channels. The people who signaled the highest intent are opportunities we're losing. We're not asking you to optimize a mature funnel. We're asking you to build one.

About the role

You own the subscription funnel from the moment a user encounters Centr through their first 30 days of paid usage. Web pages between ad click and trial start, in-app onboarding through first workout, offer architecture at trial end, cancellation, and the in-app surfaces that drive equipment upsell once they're a subscriber. You'll work next to the Sr. Ecom Manager (storefront, CRM, bundle), our growth agency (paid acquisition), and the Core UX product team (long-term in-app experience).

A dedicated full-stack web engineer is paired to you, and the two of you ship the web funnel autonomously. Paywalls and pricing iterate via RevenueCat config without dev tickets. Native mobile work routes through Core UX engineering, so part of your job is making the case for prioritization rather than assuming the capacity.

We move these numbers by building experiences worth converting on. Our read is that the funnel underperforms because the experience does, not because we haven't pushed hard enough. We'd rather earn a subscription than trap someone into one. Get the experience right and the numbers follow.

What you'll own

Web subscription onboarding. Signup, assessment, paywall, offer, trial activation. Closing the conversion gap between web and mobile is a first-90-days priority.
QR-to-app landing. The post-scan experience for retail equipment buyers (Costco, Academy) and bundle buyers.
In-app activation. Install through day 7. Onboarding flow, day-0/1/3 nudges, push, in-app engagement during trial.
Trial-to-paid conversion. Offer architecture at trial end, in-app re-engagement, cancellation on web and in-app, win-back surfaces inside the product.
Pricing and packaging. Plan architecture across iOS, Android, and web. Differentiated offers for new vs. returning vs. lapsed users.
In-app equipment upsell. The shopping feature, placement, and surfacing logic that turns subscribers into bundle and equipment buyers.

What success looks like

Web trial conversion closes a meaningful share of the gap to mobile
iOS install → paid conversion improves materially against today's baseline
A QR-to-app flow we're excited to point Costco and Academy traffic at
An in-app equipment upsell surface producing measurable attach from existing subscribers
A cancellation flow that recovers a respectable share of would-be churners
CAC payback shortened enough that paid spend can scale with confidence

You should apply if

You've owned a subscription funnel end-to-end and moved trial-to-paid at consumer scale
You've shipped against both mobile (iOS/Android) and web subscription flows and understand why they behave differently
You know where the landmines are in RevenueCat, App Store / Play Store, Stripe, and Recharge
You believe the best growth work is indistinguishable from the best product work. You move trial-to-paid by making the trial deliver value, not by hiding the cancel button
You're effective at influencing roadmaps you don't own (a meaningful chunk of your highest-leverage work lives inside the Core UX roadmap)
You spend more time in Claude Code than anyone you know

This might not be the right fit if

Your experience is all with mature, well-instrumented funnels. Building one from zero is a different muscle, and this role is mostly the zero-to-one kind
You love CRO and landing-page work but don't want to own pricing, paywalls, and trial design alongside it
You'd rather hit targets with pressure tactics than earn them through the experience
You want to own strategy and hand off execution. Here you'd do both
You want a proven playbook to run. We're still writing ours, and that's the fun of it

Why this role

Centr's subscription business has the brand, the content, the equipment, and the HYROX tailwind. What it's missing is someone to own the funnel that ties them together. If building that sounds like the best problem you could be working on, we'd like to meet you.
